questions.prompt: Why does the log give each event a sequence number instead of relying on its time to order events?
options: Sequence numbers take fewer bytes to store than timestamps
Two events can share a timestamp, but no two share a sequence number
The model needs sequence numbers to understand the conversation
Timestamps are only recorded for tool events
questions.explanation: A clock can give two events the same time, so it cannot settle their order. Sequence numbers go 1, 2, 3 with no gaps, so order is never in doubt and a missing number shows something was lost.

questions.prompt: In the example turn, an assistant/message at seq 4 lists call_1. Why is a separate tool/call event also recorded at seq 5?
options: It repeats the request in case seq 4 is lost
It records that the model has finished its reply
It records that your program actually started running the tool
It records the tool's output before the result arrives
questions.explanation: Seq 4 says what the model asked for; seq 5 says your program started the tool. If something goes wrong between them, the difference shows whether the tool ever ran.

questions.prompt: Code reading a log meets an event type it has never heard of. What is the safe thing to do?
options: Stop with an error rather than continue without it
Skip the event and carry on with the rest
Treat it as a user message so nothing is lost
Delete it from the log so it causes no further trouble
questions.explanation: Skipping an unknown fact could silently rebuild a conversation with something missing. Refusing is safer, and deleting would break the append-only rule.
